5: What does the inventory have to hold?
The data platform book's chapter, The Estate Inventory, lists a consistent set of facts for every instance it can find.
The version, edition and build number establish the support and licensing posture.
The host operating system version establishes the Arc and upgrade envelope.
The domain-join state and the owning domain establish the forest-entanglement picture.
The service account and its source domain establish the credential dependencies.
And for every database, the size, the last-access timestamp, the recovery model and the owning application establish the utilization and zombie picture that the lenses turn into a decision.
The inventory isn't a point-in-time spreadsheet.
It's designed to be re-run, because instances appear and disappear across a multi-month assessment, and the consolidation plan must track a moving estate.
6: Runbook R oh two's first step sets out the rights each depth of discovery needs.
Read access to Active Directory finds candidates; it doesn't complete the inventory.
The directory depth gives candidate hosts and instances from S P Ns and directory objects, and needs nothing more: the sequel Server Browser probe needs only a network path.
The host depth gives the instances installed and each service's account, and needs local administrator by default, or a least-privilege alternative.
The instance depth gives the version, the mode, every login and the databases, and needs a Windows login with the Start Kit's read permissions.
Azure Arc is an optional fourth depth.

Run every depth under one dedicated discovery identity per forest, a group managed service account for scheduled runs, and add the host and instance rights for the assessment window only, recording each grant and its removal.
7: Three lenses turn the inventory into a judgment.
Utilization finds zombies: a database with no connections in four hundred or more days, no restores consumed, and a retired owning application.
Version decides what can take Entra logins at all, since the FROM EXTERNAL PROVIDER syntax needs sequel Server 2022 or later.
And dependencies, such as linked servers, replication and S S I S packages, are what most often overturn a naive plan.
The result is one class per instance: retain, consolidate into a target, or retire.
One caution from R oh two.
The index-usage counters reset when the engine starts, so a database on an instance that restarted last week can look unused.
Read the start time, and take the long-horizon evidence from login auditing, backup history and the application portfolio, before you call anything a zombie.
8: The kit's classifier follows R oh two's first pass, then applies the recorded constraints.
An instance whose every database is idle past the zombie threshold, or whose every owning application is decommissioned, is retired.
An instance with no version goes to review, never to retain.
A version before sequel Server 2022 consolidates into a shared target, and 2022 or later is retained.

Collation conflicts, version-locked vendor applications, compliance isolation, indivisible dependencies and failover cluster instances turn an apparent consolidation into a dedicated target, or a retain in place.
It's a first pass: the architects confirm or override every row, and record why.
